blocks.html: In Instantaneous Velocity you found the velocity at an instant as the slope of the tangent line to an $x$–$t$ graph, and in Position, Velocity and Acceleration you met the derivative as that slope. Now we put the two together. When the position is given as a formula $x(t)$, the velocity at every instant comes from one derivative.

The velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time: $$v(t) = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\dfrac{x(t + \Delta t) - x(t)}{\Delta t}.$$ Its sign gives the direction of motion along the axis, and its size is the speed. Units: meters per second.

An average velocity $\Delta x/\Delta t$ over a long interval blurs together fast and slow stretches. Shrink the interval around one instant and the average stops changing: it settles on one number, the limit. That limit is exactly how the derivative is defined, so "velocity at an instant" and "derivative of position" are the same thing. On the graph, the secant line through two nearby points turns into the tangent line.

blocks.html: Every rule from calculus applies: the power rule, the chain rule for $\sin(\omega t)$ or $e^{-t/\tau}$, and so on. Keep the units in view. If $x$ is in meters and $t$ in seconds, then $dx/dt$ is in m/s, because a derivative is a ratio of a tiny change in $x$ to a tiny change in $t$.

steps: The sign is positive, so at that instant the particle moves in the $+x$ direction at 12 m/s.

blocks.title: When is it at rest?
blocks.q: For the same particle, when is it momentarily at rest?
steps: So $v = 0$ at $t = 1\ \text{s}$ and $t = 2\ \text{s}$. Between those times $v < 0$: the particle backs up before moving forward again.

blocks.html: Dividing the position by the time. For the particle above, $x(3)/3 = 9/3 = 3\ \text{m/s}$, but the true velocity at 3 s is 12 m/s. The ratio $x(t)/t$ is the average velocity from $t = 0$ (and only if the particle started at $x = 0$); it is not the velocity at the instant $t$. Check: the velocity at an instant must come from positions just before and just after that instant, which is what the derivative uses.

A derivative of a function you can't differentiate by hand can still be estimated: compute $\dfrac{x(t + h) - x(t - h)}{2h}$ with a small $h$, such as 0.001 s. That is how a motion sensor turns position readings into velocity.

blocks.html: Acceleration and Its Sign defined acceleration as the rate at which velocity changes. With Velocity as a Derivative in hand, that rate is one more derivative.

$$a(t) = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}.$$ Acceleration is the slope of the $v$–$t$ graph and the concavity of the $x$–$t$ graph. Its units are $(\text{m/s})/\text{s} = \text{m/s}^2$. The velocity at an instant and the acceleration at that instant are separate facts: either can be zero while the other is not.

The derivative at an instant depends on how a quantity is changing there, not on its value there. A velocity can pass through zero while it is changing quickly, like a ball at the top of its flight: just before the top its velocity is a little upward, just after it is a little downward. The change from $+$ to $-$ happens at a steady rate of $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ every second, so $a = -9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ (up positive) right through the top.

blocks.html: Newton's second law hands us the acceleration, not the position. So the usual job in mechanics runs the other way from Acceleration as a Derivative: start from $a(t)$ and work back to $v(t)$ and $x(t)$. That is antidifferentiation, and as in Antiderivatives with Initial Conditions, each step brings a constant that the starting conditions decide.

$$v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a(t')\,dt', \qquad x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t v(t')\,dt'.$$ The area under the $a$–$t$ graph from 0 to $t$ is the change in velocity; the area under the $v$–$t$ graph is the change in position.

The fundamental theorem of calculus says $\int_0^t \dfrac{dv}{dt'}\,dt' = v(t) - v(0)$. Since $dv/dt = a$, the integral of the acceleration is the change in velocity, and adding the starting velocity gives the velocity itself. In pictures: each thin strip of the $a$–$t$ graph has area $a\,\Delta t$, the small change in velocity during that sliver of time; adding up the strips gives the total change.

blocks.html: The Constant-Acceleration Equations gave you the constant-acceleration equations as tools. Velocity and Position from Acceleration lets you derive them in a few lines, and the derivation shows exactly when they are allowed.

Set $a$ equal to a constant and integrate. $$v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a\,dt' = v_0 + at.$$ Integrate again: $$x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t (v_0 + at')\,dt' = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2.$$ For the third equation, use the chain rule: $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{dx}\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$. Then $\int_{v_0}^{v} v\,dv = \int_{x_0}^{x} a\,dx$ gives $\tfrac{1}{2}v^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_0^2 = a(x - x_0)$, or $$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,\Delta x.$$

$v = v_0 + at$, $x = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ and $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$ hold only when the acceleration is constant, because pulling $a$ out of each integral assumed it never changes. When $a$ depends on time, position or velocity, integrate the real $a$ instead.

blocks.title: When the shortcut fails
blocks.q: A sled starts from rest with $a(t) = 3t$ (m/s², s). How far does it go in 2 s? Compare with $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ using $a(2)$.
steps: The acceleration grows with time, so integrate: $v(t) = \tfrac{3}{2}t^2$ and $x(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}t^3$.
The shortcut with $a(2) = 6\ \text{m/s}^2$ gives $\tfrac{1}{2}(6)(2)^2 = 12\ \text{m}$, three times too far: it pretends the sled had its final acceleration all along.
blocks.a: $4\ \text{m}$ (the constant-acceleration formula would wrongly give 12 m).

blocks.html: Using the constant-acceleration equations for a spring, air drag, a rocket burn or any force that changes. They will give a number, but a wrong one. Check before you start: is the net force, and so the acceleration, the same at every moment of the motion? If not, write $a(t)$, $a(x)$ or $a(v)$ and integrate.

One more equation falls out of the area picture: under a straight $v$–$t$ line, the area is a trapezoid, so $\Delta x = \tfrac{1}{2}(v_0 + v)t$. The average velocity is the plain average of the starting and final velocities, but only because the graph is a straight line. For a curved $v$–$t$ graph, the average velocity is $\dfrac{1}{t}\int_0^t v\,dt'$ instead.

items: Free fall without air resistance: $a = -g$, constant. The equations apply.
A block sliding down a straight frictionless ramp: $a = g\sin\theta$, constant. They apply.
A mass on a spring: $a = -(k/m)x$ changes with position. They don't.
A falling raindrop with drag: $a$ shrinks as it speeds up. They don't.

blocks.html: In Velocity and Position from Acceleration the acceleration was a function of time, so integrating over $t$ worked. But forces often depend on where an object is: a spring pulls harder the more it stretches, and gravity weakens with distance. Then $a$ is a function of $x$, and you can't integrate it over $t$ without first knowing $x(t)$, which is what you're trying to find.

The chain rule rescues us. Velocity is $v = dx/dt$, so $$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v\,\dfrac{dv}{dx}.$$ Now both sides can be written with $x$ alone: $v\,dv = a(x)\,dx$. Integrate from the starting point to the end point: $$\tfrac{1}{2}v^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_0^2 = \int_{x_0}^{x} a(x')\,dx'.$$ Time has disappeared. (Multiply by the mass and this becomes the work-energy theorem, which you'll derive in The Work-Energy Theorem from Newton's Second Law.)

When the acceleration depends on position, write $a = v\,\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ and integrate over $x$: the area under the $a$–$x$ graph equals the change in $\tfrac{1}{2}v^2$. The same trick works when $a$ depends on $v$: then $\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{a(v)}{v}$.

Notice how much simpler this is than solving for $v(t) = 10e^{-0.5t}$ first.

blocks.html: The same method handles gravity far from Earth, where $a = -GM/r^2$ depends on the distance $r$ from the planet's center. Integrating $v\,dv = -\dfrac{GM}{r^2}\,dr$ gives the speed at any height, and in Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Speed it gives the launch speed that never comes back.

Integrating $a(x)$ with respect to $t$, as in $v = \int (-4x)\,dt = -4xt$. That treats $x$ as a constant while it is changing; the result has no meaning. Check the variables: the function you integrate and the differential must match. A function of $x$ goes with $dx$, and the chain rule tells you it pairs with $v\,dv$.

blocks.html: In two or three dimensions, position is a vector that changes with time, $\vec{r}(t) = \langle x(t), y(t), z(t)\rangle$: a set of Parametric Equations. Velocity and acceleration are its derivatives, and since Adding Vectors by Components works component by component, so does calculus.

$$\vec{v} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = \left\langle \dfrac{dx}{dt}, \dfrac{dy}{dt}, \dfrac{dz}{dt} \right\rangle, \qquad \vec{a} = \dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt}.$$ The velocity is always tangent to the path, and the speed is $|\vec{v}|$. The acceleration points wherever the velocity is changing, which on a curved path is toward the inside of the curve, not along the path.

A derivative of a vector is the limit of $\Delta\vec{r}/\Delta t$, and subtracting two vectors subtracts their components. So each component is differentiated on its own. The velocity is tangent because $\Delta\vec{r}$ is a chord of the path, and chords over shorter and shorter times line up with the tangent. The acceleration is the limit of $\Delta\vec{v}/\Delta t$; when the direction of $\vec{v}$ turns, $\Delta\vec{v}$ points toward the side the path is bending, even if the speed stays the same.

blocks.html: Assuming the acceleration points along the velocity. That's only true on a straight path. A car rounding a bend at steady speed has an acceleration pointing sideways, into the bend. Check with components: if $\vec{a}$ were along $\vec{v}$, their cross product (or $v_xa_y - v_ya_x$ in two dimensions) would be zero. For the drone above, $5(12) - 8(4) = 28 \neq 0$.

blocks.html: Launched at an Angle split a launch into horizontal motion at constant velocity and vertical motion with $a = -g$. Calculus adds two powers: setting a derivative to zero finds the top of the path, and Optimization finds the angle that sends a ball farthest. Try it in the Trebuchet lab after this lesson.
With launch speed $v_0$ at angle $\theta$ from level ground (no air resistance): $$x(t) = (v_0\cos\theta)t, \qquad y(t) = (v_0\sin\theta)t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2.$$

The highest point is where $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = v_y = 0$: at $t = \dfrac{v_0\sin\theta}{g}$, with height $H = \dfrac{(v_0\sin\theta)^2}{2g}$. The range on level ground is $R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$, largest at $\theta = 45^\circ$. Launched from a height, the best angle is less than $45^\circ$.

The range comes from landing when $y = 0$ again: $t\left(v_0\sin\theta - \tfrac{1}{2}gt\right) = 0$ gives $t = 2v_0\sin\theta/g$, and $R = v_0\cos\theta \cdot 2v_0\sin\theta/g = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$. To maximize, differentiate with respect to the angle: $\dfrac{dR}{d\theta} = \dfrac{2v_0^2\cos 2\theta}{g} = 0$ when $2\theta = 90^\circ$. The second derivative is negative there, so it's a maximum. Steeper throws stay up longer but move sideways slowly; flatter throws move sideways fast but land quickly. At $45^\circ$ the trade is balanced.

blocks.html: Relative Velocity showed that velocities add as vectors when you switch viewpoints: a boat crossing a river, a plane in the wind. With Position, Velocity and Acceleration Vectors we can see exactly what changes between frames and, just as important, what doesn't.

Let frame S′ move at constant velocity $\vec{u}$ relative to frame S, with the origins together at $t = 0$. A point at $\vec{r}$ in S is at $$\vec{r}\,' = \vec{r} - \vec{u}t$$ in S′ (the Galilean transformation; time is the same in both). Differentiate once: $\vec{v}\,' = \vec{v} - \vec{u}$. Differentiate again: $\vec{a}\,' = \vec{a} - \dfrac{d\vec{u}}{dt} = \vec{a}$, because $\vec{u}$ is constant.

Frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other disagree about positions and velocities ($\vec{v}\,' = \vec{v} - \vec{u}$) but agree about accelerations. Since $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$, they also agree about forces: Newton's laws hold in every such frame. These are the inertial frames.

(Only a frame that speeds up, slows down or turns, such as a braking car, changes the acceleration, and then Newton's laws need correction terms.)
Galilean frames work at everyday speeds. Near the speed of light, time and length change between frames too, and Einstein's relativity replaces $\vec{r}\,' = \vec{r} - \vec{u}t$.

blocks.html: Centripetal Acceleration covered circles at steady speed, where $a = v^2/r$ points to the center. Position, Velocity and Acceleration Vectors showed that acceleration can point anywhere relative to the velocity. Here we split it into its two meaningful parts.

On a curved path, acceleration has two perpendicular parts: $$a_t = \dfrac{dv}{dt} \text{ (along the path)}, \qquad a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} \text{ (toward the center of curvature)},$$ and $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_c^2}$. The tangential part changes the speed; the centripetal part changes the direction.

Write the velocity as speed times a unit vector along the path, $\vec{v} = v\,\hat{T}$. The product rule gives $$\dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\hat{T} + v\,\dfrac{d\hat{T}}{dt}.$$ The first term lies along the path. For the second, on a circle of radius $r$ the unit vector $\hat{T}$ turns at the angular rate $v/r$, and a turning unit vector changes at that rate in the perpendicular direction, toward the center. So the second term has size $v \cdot v/r = v^2/r$.

The angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{v}$ tells the story at a glance: under $90^\circ$ the object is speeding up, exactly $90^\circ$ means steady speed, and over $90^\circ$ means slowing down. A car braking into a bend has an acceleration that points backward and inward at once.

The same split works on any curve, with $r$ the radius of the circle that best fits the path at that point (the radius of curvature). At the top of a projectile's arc, for example, $a_t = 0$ and $a_c = g$, so $r = v^2/g$ there.

blocks.html: Newton's Second Law Along an Axis used forces that stay the same. Real pushes rarely do: a motor ramps up, a gust fades, a bat touches a ball for a few milliseconds. Newton's second law still holds at every instant, so the acceleration simply follows the force, and Velocity and Position from Acceleration does the rest.

With a net force $F(t)$ on a mass $m$: $$a(t) = \dfrac{F(t)}{m}, \qquad v(t) = v_0 + \dfrac{1}{m}\int_0^t F(t')\,dt'.$$ The change in velocity is the area under the force–time graph divided by the mass.

$F = ma$ is a statement about one instant: the net force now sets the acceleration now. Over a tiny time $dt$ the velocity changes by $dv = a\,dt = \dfrac{F}{m}\,dt$. Adding up all those small changes is an integral. The quantity $\int F\,dt$ is the impulse, which you'll meet again in Impulse as an Integral.

blocks.html: A marble sinking through honey speeds up only briefly, then glides down at a steady pace. The fluid pushes back harder the faster the marble moves. For small, slow objects in thick fluids that drag is close to proportional to the speed, $F_D = -bv$. Newton's second law then becomes a differential equation, and the Separable Equations method solves it. It builds on Motion Under a Time-Varying Force, with a force that depends on the velocity instead of on the time.

Take down as positive. $$m\dfrac{dv}{dt} = mg - bv.$$ The speed stops changing when $mg = bv$, at the terminal speed $v_T = mg/b$. Rewrite the equation as $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{b}{m}(v_T - v)$ and separate: $$\int_0^v \dfrac{dv'}{v_T - v'} = \int_0^t \dfrac{b}{m}\,dt' \;\Rightarrow\; -\ln\dfrac{v_T - v}{v_T} = \dfrac{t}{\tau},$$ with the time constant $\tau = m/b$. Solve for $v$.

Dropped from rest with drag $-bv$: $$v(t) = v_T\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \qquad v_T = \dfrac{mg}{b}, \quad \tau = \dfrac{m}{b}.$$ The gap to terminal speed shrinks by a factor of $e$ every $\tau$: 63% of $v_T$ after one $\tau$, 95% after three, 99% after about 4.6. It never quite gets there. Coasting with no other force: $v = v_0e^{-t/\tau}$.

blocks.html: Two misreadings of terminal speed. First, the object does not stop speeding up because gravity gets weaker; $mg$ is the same all the way down. The drag grows until it matches $mg$, so the net force fades. Second, it does not reach $v_T$ at some finite time and then stop changing; it approaches it exponentially. Check with the formula: $1 - e^{-t/\tau}$ is less than 1 for every finite $t$.

For a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid, Stokes' law gives $b = 6\pi\eta r$, where $\eta$ is the fluid's viscosity and $r$ the radius. That is how the terminal speed of tiny droplets is used to measure their size. Fast objects in air feel Quadratic Drag instead.

blocks.html: Linear Drag and Terminal Velocity suits a bead in syrup. A skydiver, a baseball or a car pushes air aside, and the drag then grows with the square of the speed. You can explore its effect on launches in the Trebuchet lab, where drag pulls the best angle below 45°.

At everyday speeds in air, $$F_D = \tfrac{1}{2}C\rho Av^2,$$ where $\rho$ is the air's density (about $1.2\ \text{kg/m}^3$ near sea level), $A$ the cross-sectional area facing the flow, and $C$ the drag coefficient (about 0.3 to 0.5 for a ball, about 1 for a spread-out skydiver). Setting $F_D = mg$ gives the terminal speed $$v_T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mg}{C\rho A}}.$$

Each second, a moving object sweeps through a column of air of volume $Av$ and mass $\rho Av$, and shoves it to a speed comparable to $v$. The momentum given to the air each second, which by Newton's third law is the force back on the object, is about $(\rho Av)\cdot v = \rho Av^2$. The factor $\tfrac{1}{2}C$ captures how the shape steers the air. So doubling the speed quadruples the drag.

blocks.html: Concluding from experience in air that heavier objects fall faster in a vacuum too. Without air there is no drag, and gravity's pull $mg$ divided by the inertia $m$ gives the same $a = g$ for every mass, as astronauts showed with a hammer and a feather on the Moon. Check: in the formula for $v_T$, the mass matters only because drag exists; with $\rho = 0$, $v_T$ is infinite for everyone and all fall together.

Solving $m\,dv/dt = mg - \tfrac{1}{2}C\rho Av^2$ by separation (with partial fractions) gives $v(t) = v_T\tanh(gt/v_T)$, the curve in the picture. Unlike linear drag, the approach to $v_T$ is still exponential in the end, but the early fall looks almost like free fall, because drag is tiny at low speed.

blocks.html: Forces in Circular Motion showed that something must supply the inward force on a car rounding a curve. On a flat road only friction can. Tilting the road lets the normal force help, and Friction on Ramps gives the friction limits. You can drive one in the Circles and Gravity lab.

The car moves in a horizontal circle, so its acceleration $v^2/r$ points horizontally toward the center. Choose horizontal and vertical axes, not axes along the slope. With no friction, the normal force (perpendicular to the road, tilted toward the center by the bank angle $\theta$) has parts: $$N\cos\theta = mg \;\;(\text{vertical: no acceleration}), \qquad N\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \;\;(\text{horizontal}).$$ Dividing gives $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$.

The design speed of a curve banked at $\theta$ is $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$: there no friction is needed. Faster, friction must point down the slope; slower, up the slope. With static friction up to $\mu_sN$: $$v_{\max}^2 = rg\,\dfrac{\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}, \qquad v_{\min}^2 = rg\,\dfrac{\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta}{\cos\theta + \mu_s\sin\theta}.$$

blocks.html: Splitting the forces along and across the slope, as for a block on a ramp, and writing $N = mg\cos\theta$. On a ramp that works because the block accelerates along the slope. Here the acceleration is horizontal, so the forces across the slope don't balance; in fact $N = mg/\cos\theta$ at the design speed, larger than the weight. Check: your vertical forces must add to zero, because the car neither rises nor sinks.

Racetracks are steeply banked so cars can corner fast with little help from friction. On a road the bank is modest, because cars also crawl around the curve in traffic and must not slide down when the road is icy; that is the $v_{\min}$ condition.

blocks.html: Pulleys and the Atwood Machine handled ropes over fixed pulleys, where everything moves together at one speed. Add a pulley that moves, and the parts move at different rates. The key is one geometric fact, the rope's fixed length, turned into a statement about rates with Leibniz Notation and Units.

Write the rope's length as a sum of its straight pieces, each in terms of the positions of the objects. The total never changes, so its derivative is zero. For a load hanging from a movable pulley at height $y$, with one end tied to the ceiling (height $H$) and the other end pulled down past a fixed pulley to a hand at depth $s$ below it: $$L = 2(H - y) + s + \text{constant}.$$ Then $\dfrac{dL}{dt} = 0$ gives $\dfrac{ds}{dt} = 2\dfrac{dy}{dt}$, and once more, $a_{\text{hand}} = 2a_{\text{load}}$.

To relate accelerations in a pulley system: (1) write the rope length in terms of positions, (2) differentiate twice. A movable pulley held by two strands moves half as far, half as fast and with half the acceleration of the free end of the rope. Then write Newton's second law for each object, using the constraint to cut the unknowns.

blocks.q: A $2\ \text{kg}$ block on a frictionless table is tied to a rope that runs over a pulley at the edge, down around a movable pulley holding a $4\ \text{kg}$ block, and up to a hook under the table. Find both accelerations and the tension.
steps: Constraint: when the hanging block drops $d$, each of its two strands lengthens by $d$, so the table block slides $2d$: $a_1 = 2a_2$.
Table block: $T = m_1a_1 = 4a_2$. Hanging block: $m_2g - 2T = m_2a_2$, so $39.2 - 8a_2 = 4a_2$.

blocks.q: A $4\ \text{kg}$ load hangs from a movable pulley; the rope runs from the ceiling around it, over a fixed pulley, down to a $3\ \text{kg}$ counterweight. Find the load's acceleration.
steps: Load up $a$, counterweight down $2a$. Counterweight: $3g - T = 3(2a)$. Load: $2T - 4g = 4a$.
From the first, $T = 3g - 6a$; then $6g - 12a - 4g = 4a$, so $a = \dfrac{2g}{16} = 1.23\ \text{m/s}^2$ upward.
The lighter counterweight wins because the load is held by two strands.

blocks.html: Giving every object the same acceleration, as with a single fixed pulley. With a movable pulley, that breaks the rope: if the load and the free end both moved 1 m, two strands would have to shorten by 1 m each while only 1 m of rope came out. Check your constraint by moving one object a small distance and asking how much rope each piece gains or loses.

blocks.html: Systems and Center of Mass found the center of mass of a few separate objects as a mass-weighted average, $x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}$. A bat, a tapered beam or a rod of mixed materials is one continuous object. Slice it thin and the sums become the integrals of Moments and Centers of Mass.

Cut a rod lying on the $x$-axis into slices of width $dx$. If the linear density (mass per length) at $x$ is $\lambda(x)$, the slice there has mass $dm = \lambda(x)\,dx$ and sits at position $x$. The weighted average over infinitely many thin slices is $$x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{\int x\,dm}{\int dm} = \dfrac{\int_0^L x\lambda(x)\,dx}{\int_0^L \lambda(x)\,dx}.$$ The bottom integral is just the total mass $M$.

For a rod from $x = 0$ to $L$: $M = \int_0^L \lambda\,dx$ and $x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{1}{M}\int_0^L x\lambda\,dx$. Uniform rods balance at the middle; a rod that gets denser toward one end balances closer to that end.

blocks.html: Two slips: forgetting to divide by $M$ (then the "position" comes out in kg·m), or integrating $x\,dx$ without the density (which finds the middle of a uniform rod whatever the real density is). Check the units: $\int x\lambda\,dx$ is in kg·m, $M$ in kg, so $x_{\text{cm}}$ is in meters. And check the range: the answer must lie between 0 and $L$, nearer the denser end.

Why care where the center of mass is? Because the whole object's motion is simplest there: gravity acts as if it pulled at that one point, a thrown bat spins around it while it follows a clean parabola, and Newton's Second Law for a System shows that the external forces alone decide how it accelerates. You'll also need $\int x^2\,dm$, a close cousin of $\int x\,dm$, for Moment of Inertia by Integration.

The same idea works in two and three dimensions, one coordinate at a time: $y_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{1}{M}\int y\,dm$. Symmetry often saves work: a uniform disk, ring or sphere has its center of mass at its geometric center.

blocks.html: Work as Area Under a Force Graph found work as the area under a force–position graph, using triangles and rectangles. With Evaluating Integrals with FTC Part 2 you can find that area for any force you can write as a formula.

The work done by a force $F(x)$ along the $x$-axis from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is $$W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x)\,dx,$$ the signed area under the $F$–$x$ curve, in joules (N·m). For a spring stretched by an outside force $F = kx$: $W = \tfrac{1}{2}k\left(x_2^2 - x_1^2\right)$.

Over a short step $\Delta x$ the force hardly changes, so the work on that step is about $F(x)\Delta x$, the area of a thin rectangle. The total is the sum of those pieces, $\sum F(x_i)\Delta x$, a Riemann sum. Making the steps thinner turns the sum into the integral. When $F$ is constant, the integral is just $F\,\Delta x$, the rule you already know.

blocks.html: Work by a Variable Force handled motion along a straight line with the force along that line. Now let the path curve and the force point any way. The tool is The Dot Product and the Angle Between Vectors: it keeps only the part of the force along each little step.

$$W = \int_{\text{path}} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = \int \left(F_x\,dx + F_y\,dy + F_z\,dz\right).$$ Only the component of $\vec{F}$ along the direction of motion does work. For a straight path and a constant force, $W = \vec{F}\cdot\Delta\vec{r} = F\,d\cos\theta$.

Break the path into tiny straight steps $d\vec{r}$. On one step the force is nearly constant, and the work is $\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = F\,dr\cos\theta$: a force perpendicular to the step ($\theta = 90^\circ$) does nothing, a force along it does the most. Add up the steps and you have a line integral. To compute it, describe the path with one parameter, such as $x$ or $t$, and write $dx$, $dy$ and the force in terms of it.

blocks.html: The Work-Energy Theorem stated that the net work on an object equals its change in kinetic energy. With the chain-rule trick from Acceleration That Depends on Position and the work integral from Work by a Variable Force, you can prove it from Newton's second law in three lines.

Start from $\Sigma F = m\dfrac{dv}{dt}$ along the line of motion. Rewrite the acceleration with the chain rule: $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{dx}\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$. So $\Sigma F = mv\dfrac{dv}{dx}$. Integrate both sides over the motion: $$\int_{x_1}^{x_2} \Sigma F\,dx = \int_{v_1}^{v_2} mv\,dv = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_2^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_1^2.$$ The left side is the net work; the right side is the change in $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. In three dimensions the same steps work with $\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$.

$$W_{\text{net}} = \int \Sigma\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = \Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_2^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_1^2.$$ It holds for any forces, constant or not. "Net" matters: add the work of every force, or integrate the net force.

blocks.html: Why bother, when $F = ma$ already holds? Because the theorem answers "how fast at this place?" without ever finding $x(t)$, which for a force that depends on position can be hard or impossible to write down. It also splits naturally: conservative forces' work moves into potential energy (Potential Energy from Force), and what's left is the work of everything else.

Using the work of one force, often the applied push, as if it were the net work. In the first example the push alone does $120\ \text{J}$, which would predict $v = 7\ \text{m/s}$, ignoring the $39.2\ \text{J}$ friction takes back. blocks.html: Work Along a Path showed a force whose work changed when the path changed. Gravity is different: lift a book straight up or carry it up the stairs, and gravity does the same work either way. That difference sorts all forces into two kinds.

A force is conservative when the work it does between two points is the same along every path; equivalently, its work around every closed loop is zero. Gravity, ideal springs and the electric force between charges are conservative. Friction and drag are not: their work depends on the length of the path, and around a loop it is negative.

The two definitions are the same statement. Go from A to B along path 1 and come back along path 2: the loop's work is $W_1 - W_2$, since reversing a path flips the sign of each $\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$. That is zero for every loop exactly when $W_1 = W_2$ for every pair of paths. For gravity near Earth, $\vec{F} = \langle 0, -mg \rangle$, so $W = \int -mg\,dy = -mg\,\Delta y$, which depends only on the heights of the ends. Friction always points against the motion, so every step of every path adds negative work, and longer paths add more.

blocks.cap: The field $\langle -y, x \rangle$ pushes along the circle at every point, so the work around the loop is $2\pi$, not zero.

blocks.q: A $2\ \text{kg}$ ball moves from a height of $5\ \text{m}$ to a height of $1\ \text{m}$, once by falling straight down and once along a winding slide. Find gravity's work each way.

blocks.title: Friction on two paths
blocks.q: A $5\ \text{kg}$ box is slid across a floor ($\mu_k = 0.2$) between opposite corners of a $3\ \text{m}$ by $4\ \text{m}$ rectangle, once along two sides and once along the diagonal. Find friction's work each way.
steps: Friction's size is $\mu_kmg = 0.2(5)(9.8) = 9.8\ \text{N}$, always against the motion, so $W = -9.8\ \text{N} \times (\text{path length})$.
Along two sides: $-9.8(7) = -68.6\ \text{J}$. Along the diagonal: $-9.8(5) = -49\ \text{J}$.
Different paths, different work: friction is not conservative.
blocks.a: $-68.6\ \text{J}$ along the sides; $-49\ \text{J}$ along the diagonal.

blocks.html: Treating friction like gravity, as if it did the same work on any route between two points. Friction's work grows with the distance traveled, not with the displacement; drag a box around a room and back to its spot, and friction has done plenty of negative work while gravity has done none. Check: ask whether the force does negative work on every piece of a round trip. If so, it can't be conservative.

A test without drawing paths: in two dimensions, a force $\langle F_x, F_y \rangle$ defined on a region without holes is conservative exactly when $\dfrac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial F_y}{\partial x}$. For $\langle -y, x \rangle$ these are $-1$ and $1$, so it fails. For a conservative force you can then find a potential energy, as in Potential Energy from Force.

blocks.html: Because a conservative force's work depends only on the endpoints (Conservative Forces), we can keep track of it with a function of position alone: the potential energy. This lesson builds $U(x)$ from the force.

For a conservative force $F(x)$, choose a reference point $x_0$ where $U = 0$. Then $$U(x) = -\int_{x_0}^{x} F(x')\,dx', \qquad \Delta U = -W_{\text{force}}.$$ Spring ($F = -kx$, $x_0 = 0$): $U = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$. Uniform gravity ($F_y = -mg$, $y_0 = 0$): $U = mgy$. Universal gravity ($F = -GMm/r^2$, $U = 0$ at $r \to \infty$): $U = -GMm/r$.

We want $U$ to store the energy the force can give back. When the force does positive work, it hands energy to the object's motion, so the stored energy must go down by the same amount: $\Delta U = -W$. Writing the work as an integral gives the formula. The minus sign is the whole point: a spring force pulls back toward $x = 0$, so stretching it means the force does negative work, and $U$ goes up. Only differences in $U$ matter physically; the reference point is a free choice, and changing it adds the same constant everywhere.

blocks.name: ph-energy

opts.task: Drag the energy line. The ball turns around where it meets the curve $U = 2x^2$.

blocks.cap: The potential energy of a spring with $k = 4\ \text{N/m}$: $U = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = 2x^2$. It rises on both sides because the force always points back toward $x = 0$.

blocks.title: A spring
blocks.q: Find $U(x)$ for a spring with $F = -kx$, taking $U(0) = 0$.
steps: $U(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$. Check: it is zero at natural length and positive for stretching or squeezing.

blocks.title: Gravity far from Earth
blocks.q: Gravity pulls a mass $m$ toward Earth's center with $F(r) = -\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$. Find $U(r)$ with $U = 0$ as $r \to \infty$.
steps: Negative everywhere, rising toward zero far away: it takes work to pull the mass out to where $U = 0$.

blocks.html: Dropping the minus sign. Without it, a spring's "potential energy" would be $-\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, falling as you stretch the spring, as if a stretched spring had less stored energy than a relaxed one. Check the direction: when you move against a force, the potential energy must rise. Also check that $-dU/dx$ gives back $F$; you'll use that in Force from Potential Energy.
Friction has no potential energy: its work depends on the path, so there is no function of position alone that could keep track of it. Its work goes into thermal energy instead.

blocks.html: Potential Energy from Force built $U$ by integrating the force. Run it backward with Leibniz Notation and Units and the force comes from $U$ by differentiating. This is how physicists usually work: write down an energy, and the forces follow.

$$F(x) = -\dfrac{dU}{dx}.$$ The force points downhill on the $U(x)$ graph, toward lower potential energy, and it is strongest where the graph is steepest. In three dimensions, $\vec{F} = -\nabla U = -\left\langle \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial x}, \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial y}, \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial z} \right\rangle$.

Over a tiny step $dx$, the force does work $F\,dx$, and the potential energy changes by $dU = -F\,dx$. Divide by $dx$: $F = -dU/dx$. Picture a ball on a hilly track shaped like the $U$ graph: it is pushed toward the valleys, harder where the slope is steep, and not at all at a flat spot.

blocks.name: derivgraph

opts.task: Read the top graph as $U(x)$. The force is the bottom graph with its sign flipped: where $U$ rises, the force points left.

blocks.cap: $U(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2$ on top and $dU/dx$ below. At $x = 1$, $dU/dx = -3$, so $F = +3\ \text{N}$, pushing toward $+x$, downhill.

blocks.title: Force at a point
blocks.q: A particle has $U(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2$ (J, m). Find the force on it at $x = 1\ \text{m}$ and at $x = 3\ \text{m}$.

blocks.title: A model chemical bond
blocks.q: A simple model of a bond has $U(x) = \dfrac{4}{x^2} - \dfrac{4}{x}$ (energy and distance in convenient units). Where is the force zero, and which way does it push when the atoms are closer than that?
steps: For $x < 2$, $8/x^3 > 4/x^2$, so $F > 0$: the atoms are pushed apart. For $x > 2$ they are pulled together.
blocks.a: Zero at $x = 2$; closer than that, the force pushes the atoms apart.

blocks.html: Thinking the force points toward higher potential energy, the way a dropped ball "heads for" the ground. The ball does head downhill on the $U$ graph: lower height, lower $U$. Check with gravity: $U = mgy$ gives $F_y = -mg$, pointing down, toward lower $U$. If your force points uphill on the $U$ graph, you dropped the minus sign.
Where $dU/dx = 0$ the force vanishes: those are the equilibrium points. Whether an object placed there stays put depends on the shape of $U$ around it, the subject of Potential Energy Diagrams.

blocks.html: A graph of $U(x)$ with a horizontal line at the total energy $E$ tells you nearly everything about one-dimensional motion without solving any equation. It combines Force from Potential Energy (force is minus the slope) with Concavity and the Second Derivative Test (the shape of a graph near a flat point).

With total energy $E$, the kinetic energy is $K = E - U(x)$, the gap between the line and the curve.
  • Allowed regions: where $U(x) \le E$, since $K$ can't be negative.
  • Turning points: where $U(x) = E$; the object stops and reverses.
  • Equilibria: where $dU/dx = 0$. A minimum ($d^2U/dx^2 > 0$) is stable; a maximum ($d^2U/dx^2 < 0$) is unstable.

Energy conservation says $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + U(x) = E$, so $v = \pm\sqrt{2(E - U)/m}$: fastest where $U$ is lowest, zero where $U = E$. At a minimum of $U$, a small nudge either way puts the object uphill, and the force $-dU/dx$ points back toward the minimum: it rocks back and forth there (stable). At a maximum, a nudge puts it downhill, and the force pushes it farther away (unstable).

opts.task: Drag the energy line above and below the hump at $x = 0$. Below it, the ball stays in one well.

blocks.cap: The double well $U = x^4 - 8x^2$ with $E = -7\ \text{J}$: the ball is trapped between $x = 1$ and $x = \sqrt{7}$ in the right-hand well.

blocks.title: Equilibria of a double well
blocks.q: Find and classify the equilibria of $U(x) = x^4 - 8x^2$ (J, m).
steps: $\dfrac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 12x^2 - 16$: at $x = 0$ it is $-16$ (a maximum, unstable); at $x = \pm 2$ it is $32$ (minima, stable).

blocks.title: Turning points
blocks.q: A particle in the same well has $E = -7\ \text{J}$ and starts in the right-hand well. Where does it turn around?
steps: Between them $U < E$; outside them $U > E$, which is forbidden. Since $E < U(0) = 0$, it can't cross to the left well.

blocks.html: Thinking the object can pass through a region where $E < U$, perhaps "with enough momentum." Its momentum is already counted in $E$. Where $U > E$, the kinetic energy $E - U$ would be negative, and $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ can't be. Check by reading the graph: if the energy line is below the curve somewhere, the object can't get there from where it is (in classical physics; quantum tunneling is a different story, met in later physics).

Near a stable minimum, any smooth $U$ looks like a parabola, $U \approx U_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}U''(x_0)(x - x_0)^2$: a spring with $k = U''(x_0)$. That is why small oscillations everywhere in nature are close to simple harmonic, as you'll see in The Equation of Simple Harmonic Motion.

blocks.html: Power defined power as work per time, $P = W/\Delta t$, and showed $P = Fv$ for a steady push. With Work by a Variable Force, power becomes the rate of work at each instant, even when the force and speed change.

$$P = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}.$$ The power of the net force equals $\dfrac{dK}{dt}$. Units: watts (J/s). The total work over a time interval is the area under the $P$–$t$ graph, $W = \int P\,dt$.

In a tiny time $dt$ the object moves $d\vec{r} = \vec{v}\,dt$, so the force does work $dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}\,dt$. Divide by $dt$. A force perpendicular to the velocity, like the tension on a ball whirled in a circle at steady speed, delivers zero power: it changes the direction, never the speed.

opts.task: A steady $500\ \text{N}$ push accelerates a $250\ \text{kg}$ cart from rest. The power grows as the speed does; the area is the work.

blocks.cap: With a constant force from rest, $v = (F/m)t$, so $P = Fv = \dfrac{F^2}{m}t$ grows linearly: $1000t$ watts here. The area over 10 s is $50\ \text{kJ} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

blocks.title: Cruising against drag
blocks.q: A car cruises at $25\ \text{m/s}$, with air drag and rolling resistance adding up to $500\ \text{N}$. What power reaches the wheels?
steps: At steady speed the driving force equals the resistance, $500\ \text{N}$, along the velocity.

blocks.title: Constant power from rest
blocks.q: A $1000\ \text{kg}$ car's engine delivers a steady $50\ \text{kW}$ starting from rest. Ignoring losses, when does it reach $20\ \text{m/s}$?
steps: The force $P/v$ is enormous at first and falls as the car speeds up: the acceleration is not constant.

blocks.html: Using the average power when the force or speed is changing. For the cart in the picture, the average power over 10 s is $5\ \text{kW}$, but at the end the push delivers $10\ \text{kW}$, twice as much. The average $W/\Delta t$ tells you the total energy per time; the instantaneous $\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$ tells you the rate right now. Check: if $v$ changes during the interval, the two will differ.

The same idea carries over to turning: a torque $\tau$ on something spinning at $\omega$ delivers $P = \tau\omega$, which you'll derive in Work and Power in Rotation. An engine's power rating is a torque times a rotation rate.

Drag force grows like $v^2$, so the power to overcome it grows like $v^3$: driving 10% faster takes about $1.1^3 \approx 1.33$ times the power against drag. That is one reason fuel use rises quickly at highway speeds.

blocks.html: Gravitational Potential Energy Far from Earth gave the potential energy $U = -GMm/r$, and Potential Energy from Force derived it by integrating Newton's gravity from infinity. Now use it to answer an old question: how fast must something be launched so that it never falls back? Build and fly a rocket in the Rocket Builder lab to see the numbers at work.

Ignore the air. After launch, only gravity acts, so $K + U$ stays constant: $$\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = E.$$ As the object climbs, $U$ rises toward 0 and $K$ falls. If $E < 0$, then $K$ would have to become negative before $r$ reaches infinity, which can't happen: the object stops and falls back. If $E \ge 0$, it can reach any distance with $K \ge 0$ to spare. The boundary is $E = 0$: $$\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\text{esc}}^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{R}.$$

From a distance $r$ from a body's center, $$v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}},$$ independent of the mass of the object launched. From Earth's surface it is about $11.2\ \text{km/s}$. Launched faster, the object coasts away with $v_\infty = \sqrt{v_0^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2}$.

blocks.html: Thinking a heavier object needs a higher escape speed. It needs more energy, since both $K$ and $U$ are proportional to $m$, but the mass cancels from the speed. A grain of sand and a spacecraft need the same 11.2 km/s from Earth's surface. Check: the formula $\sqrt{2GM/r}$ contains the planet's mass, not the projectile's.

Real rockets don't fire once at escape speed from the ground; they burn for minutes, climb out of the thick air, and usually go into orbit first. Escape speed is still the energy budget they must reach: $E \ge 0$.

blocks.html: Impulse and Change in Momentum wrote impulse as $F\Delta t$ and found it as the area under a force–time graph. Real collisions don't have a constant force: a bat's push rises from zero to a peak and falls back in a millisecond or two. Evaluating Integrals with FTC Part 2 handles any shape.

$$\vec{J} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \vec{F}\,dt = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_2 - m\vec{v}_1.$$ The impulse is the area under the $F$–$t$ curve, in N·s (the same as kg·m/s). The average force over the contact is $F_{\text{avg}} = J/\Delta t$.

Newton's second law in its original form says $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$: force is the rate of change of momentum. Integrate both sides over the collision: $\int \vec{F}\,dt = \int d\vec{p} = \Delta\vec{p}$. Nothing about the force's shape was assumed, so a spike, a smooth bump or a wobbly curve all work, as long as you integrate the real force.

blocks.title: A bounce
blocks.q: A $0.1\ \text{kg}$ ball hits a wall at $15\ \text{m/s}$ and rebounds at $10\ \text{m/s}$ after $0.005\ \text{s}$ of contact, with a half-sine force $F_{\max}\sin(\pi t/T)$. Find the peak force.
steps: With the rebound direction positive, $\Delta p = 0.1(10) - 0.1(-15) = 2.5\ \text{N·s}$: the speeds add, because the direction reverses.
The average force is $2.5/0.005 = 500\ \text{N}$, about 64% of the peak.

blocks.html: Multiplying the peak force by the collision time. For the baseball that gives $1000 \times 0.01 = 10\ \text{N·s}$, 57% too much, because the force is near its peak only briefly. The right rectangle uses the average force, which you can only find after integrating. Check with the graph: a rectangle drawn at the peak height always encloses more area than the curve under it.
This is the physics of padding: a soft surface spreads the same $\Delta p$ over a longer time, so the area stays the same while the peak force drops.

blocks.html: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions defined an elastic collision as one that keeps the total kinetic energy. Solving one means handling two equations at once, one of them quadratic, which is a job for Nonlinear Systems. A clever division turns it into two linear equations.

For masses $m_1, m_2$ with velocities $v_1, v_2$ before and $v_1', v_2'$ after, move each object's terms to its own side: $$m_1(v_1 - v_1') = m_2(v_2' - v_2) \quad\text{(momentum)},$$ $$m_1(v_1^2 - v_1'^2) = m_2(v_2'^2 - v_2^2) \quad\text{(kinetic energy, times 2)}.$$ Factor the squares, $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$, and divide the second equation by the first (the collision happened, so $v_1 \ne v_1'$): $$v_1 + v_1' = v_2 + v_2' \;\Rightarrow\; v_2' - v_1' = -(v_2 - v_1).$$

In a one-dimensional elastic collision, the relative velocity reverses: the objects separate as fast as they approached. Together with momentum conservation, that gives $$v_1' = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_1 + \dfrac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_2, \qquad v_2' = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_1 + \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_2.$$

blocks.q: A $2\ \text{kg}$ glider at $6\ \text{m/s}$ collides elastically with a $4\ \text{kg}$ glider at rest. Find both velocities afterward.

blocks.html: Writing only the momentum equation. With two unknown final velocities, one equation can't decide them; any pair on a line works, including ones that create energy. Check: count unknowns and equations. For an elastic collision use momentum plus the reversal of relative velocity (which is energy conservation in disguise); for a perfectly inelastic one, use momentum plus "same final velocity."

A very heavy object hitting a light one at rest: the light one leaves at nearly $2v_1$.
A light object hitting a very heavy one at rest: it bounces back at nearly its original speed.

blocks.html: Conservation of Momentum said that with no net outside force, total momentum stays the same. Momentum is a vector, so in a plane that one statement is two equations, one for each direction.

In a collision with negligible outside forces, $$\sum p_x \text{ before} = \sum p_x \text{ after}, \qquad \sum p_y \text{ before} = \sum p_y \text{ after}.$$ Solve them like any two equations; then rebuild speeds and angles from the components. Kinetic energy is conserved only if the collision is elastic.

During the brief contact, the objects push on each other with equal and opposite forces (Newton's third law), so their impulses on each other cancel as vectors. Outside forces like friction act too, but over a few milliseconds their impulse is tiny. A vector that doesn't change has components that don't change, so each direction is conserved on its own.

blocks.title: Cars at an intersection
blocks.q: A $1200\ \text{kg}$ car heading east at $15\ \text{m/s}$ and a $2000\ \text{kg}$ truck heading north at $10\ \text{m/s}$ collide and lock together. Find the speed and direction of the wreck.

blocks.title: Equal masses, elastic
blocks.q: A billiard ball hits an identical ball at rest, off center and elastically. The first ball leaves at $30^\circ$ to its original line. In what direction does the second go?
steps: Momentum (the masses cancel): $\vec{v}_0 = \vec{v}_1 + \vec{v}_2$. Energy: $v_0^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2$.
Square the momentum equation: $v_0^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2 + 2\vec{v}_1\cdot\vec{v}_2$. Compare: $\vec{v}_1\cdot\vec{v}_2 = 0$.
The balls leave at right angles, so the second goes at $60^\circ$ on the other side of the original line.

blocks.html: Is energy conserved too? Compare: the car and truck had $\tfrac{1}{2}(1200)(15)^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(2000)(10)^2 = 235\ \text{kJ}$ before and $\tfrac{1}{2}(3200)(8.41)^2 = 113\ \text{kJ}$ after. More than half went into crumpling metal, heat and sound, as expected when objects stick. Momentum is conserved in every collision; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.

Conserving the total speed, or adding magnitudes of momentum as if they were numbers. In the intersection crash, $18\,000 + 20\,000 = 38\,000\ \text{kg·m/s}$ would give $11.9\ \text{m/s}$, but the momenta are perpendicular and add like the sides of a right triangle. Check: write the $x$ and $y$ equations separately, with signs, and only combine them into a magnitude at the very end.

blocks.html: Motion of the Center of Mass showed that with no outside force, a system's center of mass coasts at constant velocity. Center of Mass by Integration located the center of mass of anything. Now the general rule: what external forces do to it.

For each particle $i$, $m_i\vec{a}_i = \vec{F}_i^{\text{ext}} + \sum_j \vec{F}_{ij}$, where $\vec{F}_{ij}$ is the force particle $j$ exerts on particle $i$. Add over all particles. The left side is $\sum m_i\vec{a}_i = M\vec{a}_{\text{cm}}$, since $M\vec{r}_{\text{cm}} = \sum m_i\vec{r}_i$ differentiated twice. On the right, every internal force $\vec{F}_{ij}$ appears with its third-law partner $\vec{F}_{ji} = -\vec{F}_{ij}$, so they cancel in pairs. Only the external forces survive.

$$\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = M\vec{a}_{\text{cm}}.$$ The center of mass moves like a single particle of mass $M$ acted on by the external forces alone, however the parts push, pull, spin or break apart.

If the boat moves back $d$, the person moves forward $4 - d$ relative to the water: $60(4 - d) = 140d$.

The internal forces still matter for how each part moves, just not for the center of mass.

blocks.html: A rocket in empty space has nothing to push against, yet it speeds up. It does it by throwing mass backward, a steady stream of Newton's Second Law for a System in action. Adding up the tiny kicks takes the logarithm from Integrals Giving Exponentials and Logarithms. Build one in the Rocket Builder lab.

Watch from a frame moving with the rocket at one instant. In a short time the rocket (mass $m$) throws out a little exhaust, of mass $|dm|$, backward at speed $v_e$ relative to itself. Momentum in that frame starts at zero and stays zero, so the rocket gains $dv$ with $$m\,dv = v_e\,|dm| = -v_e\,dm,$$ since the rocket's mass is decreasing ($dm < 0$). Separate and integrate from the starting mass $m_0$ to the final mass $m_f$: $$\int dv = -v_e\int_{m_0}^{m_f} \dfrac{dm}{m} = v_e\ln\dfrac{m_0}{m_f}.$$ The push on the rocket is the momentum given to the exhaust each second: $F_{\text{thrust}} = v_e\left|\dfrac{dm}{dt}\right|$.

$$\Delta v = v_e\ln\dfrac{m_0}{m_f}, \qquad F_{\text{thrust}} = v_e\left|\dfrac{dm}{dt}\right|.$$ The speed gained depends only on the exhaust speed and the mass ratio, not on how fast the fuel burns. Because of the logarithm, each extra bit of $\Delta v$ needs an exponentially larger mass ratio, $m_0/m_f = e^{\Delta v/v_e}$.

blocks.q: A rocket in deep space is 80% fuel, with exhaust speed $3000\ \text{m/s}$. What is its $\Delta v$ when all the fuel is burned?

blocks.q: A spacecraft with $v_e = 3000\ \text{m/s}$ needs $\Delta v = 6000\ \text{m/s}$. What fraction of its starting mass must be fuel?
steps: Fuel fraction $= 1 - 1/7.39 = 0.865$, so 86.5% of the starting mass is fuel.
Doubling the $\Delta v$ again would need $e^4 \approx 55$: hence multistage rockets, which drop empty tanks along the way.

blocks.html: Thinking a rocket moves by pushing against the air or the launch pad. It works best in a vacuum, where there is nothing to push on at all. Check with momentum: the system "rocket plus exhaust" has no outside force in deep space, so if the exhaust gains backward momentum, the rocket must gain the same forward momentum. The push comes from the exhaust gas, which the rocket shoves backward and which shoves the rocket forward.

Near the ground, gravity also acts, so the rocket must have thrust larger than its weight to lift off, and $F_{\text{thrust}} - mg = ma$ gives its acceleration. The acceleration grows as fuel burns, since $m$ shrinks while the thrust stays about the same.

blocks.html: Rotational Kinematics handled spinning with constant angular acceleration. Everything you did in Velocity and Position from Acceleration carries over to rotation with one change of letters: $x \to \theta$, $v \to \omega$, $a \to \alpha$.

$$\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}, \qquad \alpha = \dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}, \qquad \omega(t) = \omega_0 + \int_0^t \alpha\,dt'.$$ Angles in radians, $\omega$ in rad/s, $\alpha$ in rad/s². Every point of a rigid body shares the same $\theta$, $\omega$ and $\alpha$.

A radian is defined as arc length divided by radius, $\theta = s/r$, so it is a pure number and $s = r\theta$ holds exactly. Differentiating gives $v = r\omega$ and $a_t = r\alpha$ for a point at distance $r$ from the axis. Those simple links, and the formulas for rotational energy and work built on them, only hold with angles measured in radians.

blocks.html: Rotational Inertia defined $I = \sum mr^2$ for point masses: mass far from the axis counts more. For a solid object, slice it into tiny pieces as in Center of Mass by Integration and add up $r^2\,dm$.

$$I = \int r^2\,dm,$$ where $r$ is each piece's distance from the axis of rotation. Results worth knowing: thin rod about its center $\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$, about one end $\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2$; thin hoop $MR^2$; solid disk or cylinder about its axle $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$; solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$; thin spherical shell $\tfrac{2}{3}MR^2$.

Kinetic energy explains the $r^2$. A piece at distance $r$ moves at $v = r\omega$, so its energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}dm\,(r\omega)^2$. Adding over the body: $K = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\int r^2\,dm\right)\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. Doubling a piece's distance from the axis doubles its speed and quadruples its energy at the same $\omega$.

blocks.html: Moment of Inertia by Integration gave $I$ about axes through the center of mass. Objects often turn about other axes: a door on its hinges, a pendulum on a pin, a disk swinging from its rim. One theorem saves you from integrating again.

If $I_{\text{cm}}$ is the moment of inertia about an axis through the center of mass, then about any parallel axis a distance $d$ away, $$I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2.$$ The center-of-mass axis gives the smallest $I$ of all parallel axes.

Put the center of mass at the origin and the new axis at $x = -d$ (parallel to the old one). A piece at $x$ is now a distance $x + d$ along that direction from the axis: $$I = \int (x + d)^2\,dm = \int x^2\,dm + 2d\int x\,dm + d^2\int dm.$$ The first term is $I_{\text{cm}}$ (the other coordinate's contribution is the same for both axes). The middle term vanishes, because $\int x\,dm = Mx_{\text{cm}} = 0$ at the center of mass. The last term is $Md^2$. The cancellation only happens when you start from the center of mass.

blocks.html: Torque measured turning effect as $\tau = rF\sin\theta$. The The Cross Product packages that size together with a direction, which you need as soon as forces don't all lie in one plane.

The torque about a point O of a force $\vec{F}$ applied at position $\vec{r}$ (measured from O to where the force acts) is $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}, \qquad |\vec{\tau}| = rF\sin\theta.$$ Its direction, by the right-hand rule, is along the axis the force tends to turn the object about. In a plane, $\tau_z = r_xF_y - r_yF_x$: positive is counterclockwise seen from $+z$.

Torque should grow with the force and with the lever arm, and only the part of the force perpendicular to $\vec{r}$ should turn anything; pushing straight toward the pivot does nothing. The cross product has exactly these properties: its size is $rF\sin\theta$, zero when $\vec{F}$ is along $\vec{r}$. And its direction answers "turning about which axis, and which way?" in one vector, which lets torques from different directions add as vectors.

Check: $\vec{\tau}\cdot\vec{r} = 8 - 8 + 0 = 0$ and $\vec{\tau}\cdot\vec{F} = 0 - 12 + 12 = 0$. The torque is perpendicular to both, as a cross product must be.

blocks.html: Because torques are vectors, several of them add component by component, and an object is in rotational equilibrium only when all three components of the total are zero. In Static Equilibrium Problems you'll pick the point about which to take torques so that unknown forces drop out.

Two slips: measuring $\vec{r}$ from the origin when the torque is wanted about another point, and reversing the order. About a point Q, use $\vec{r} = \vec{r}_{\text{force}} - \vec{r}_Q$; the same force has different torques about different points. And $\vec{F}\times\vec{r} = -\vec{r}\times\vec{F}$, so the wrong order flips every sign. Check with the right-hand rule: curl your fingers the way the force would turn the object; your thumb must point along $\vec{\tau}$.

blocks.html: Rolling Without Slipping showed with energy that a hoop loses a race down a ramp to a solid ball. Newton's Second Law for Rotation lets us find the forces and the acceleration directly, and see what static friction is doing.

Take an object of mass $M$, radius $R$ and $I = cMR^2$ rolling down a ramp at angle $\theta$. Along the ramp: $$Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma.$$ About the center, only friction has a lever arm: $$fR = I\alpha = cMR^2\alpha.$$ Rolling without slipping links them: $a = R\alpha$. So $f = cMa$, and substituting, $Mg\sin\theta = Ma(1 + c)$.

$$a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/(MR^2)}, \qquad f = \dfrac{I}{R^2}a.$$ Mass and radius cancel; only the shape factor $c = I/(MR^2)$ matters: solid ball 0.4, solid disk 0.5, hollow ball 0.67, hoop 1. Static friction must supply $f$, so rolling needs $\mu_s \ge \dfrac{c}{1 + c}\tan\theta$.

blocks.html: Why don't mass and radius matter? A bigger or heavier object of the same shape has more weight pulling it down the ramp, but proportionally more inertia, both for moving and for spinning. Only the shape, through $I/(MR^2)$, decides how the energy splits between moving and spinning.

Thinking static friction drains energy from a rolling object, so energy conservation fails. The contact point of a rolling object is momentarily at rest ($v_{\text{contact}} = v - R\omega = 0$), so friction acting there does no work. It moves energy from "moving" to "spinning" without losing any. Check: the energy method above, which ignores friction, gives the same answer as the force method, which includes it. blocks.html: Rolling Dynamics assumed rolling without slipping from the start. A bowling ball doesn't begin that way: it lands on the lane sliding, with almost no spin. Kinetic friction then works on it until it rolls.

While the ball slides, kinetic friction $\mu_kMg$ acts backward at the contact point. It slows the center, $v = v_0 - \mu_kgt$, and its torque $\mu_kMgR$ spins the ball up: for a solid ball ($I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$), $R\omega = \tfrac{5}{2}\mu_kgt$. Sliding stops when $v = R\omega$: $$v_0 - \mu_kgt = \tfrac{5}{2}\mu_kgt \;\Rightarrow\; t = \dfrac{2v_0}{7\mu_kg}, \quad v = \tfrac{5}{7}v_0.$$ A slicker route: friction acts at the contact point and gravity balances the normal force, so angular momentum about any point on the floor stays constant: $Mv_0R = MvR + I\omega$ gives the same $\tfrac{5}{7}v_0$ in one line, without $\mu_k$.

An object launched sliding with no spin skids until $v = R\omega$, then rolls at $v = \dfrac{v_0}{1 + I/(MR^2)}$: $\tfrac{5}{7}v_0$ for a solid ball, $\tfrac{2}{3}v_0$ for a disk, $\tfrac{1}{2}v_0$ for a hoop. During the skid, kinetic friction turns kinetic energy into heat; once it rolls, that stops.

Backspin ($\omega_0 < 0$) makes the final speed smaller; enough topspin can make the ball speed up as friction grips.

blocks.html: Angular Momentum and Angular Impulse used $L = I\omega$ for spinning objects and $L = mvr_\perp$ for a point mass going by. With Torque as a Cross Product, both come from one vector definition.

The angular momentum of a particle about a point O is $$\vec{L} = \vec{r}\times\vec{p} = m\,\vec{r}\times\vec{v},$$ with $\vec{r}$ measured from O. Its size is $mvr\sin\phi = mvd$, where $d$ is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of motion. Newton's second law gives $\dfrac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{\tau}$.

Differentiate with the product rule: $\dfrac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt}\times\vec{p} + \vec{r}\times\dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v}\times m\vec{v} + \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$. The first term is zero (a vector crossed with itself), and the second is the torque. So with no torque, $\vec{L}$ is constant. A free particle moving in a straight line has no force, so no torque about any point, and its angular momentum about any point never changes, even though it doesn't go around anything.

blocks.html: Thinking a particle needs to move in a circle to have angular momentum. Any motion that doesn't head straight at (or away from) the point has some. A meteor flying past the Earth, a ball thrown past a door's hinge, a puck sliding past a post: each carries $mvd$ about that point. Check: compute $\vec{r}\times\vec{p}$. It is zero only if $\vec{v}$ points along $\vec{r}$, toward or away from the point.

For a rigid body spinning about a fixed axis, add up $\vec{r}\times m\vec{v}$ over all its pieces: each piece has $v = r\omega$ around the axis, and the axial part of the total is $\sum mr^2\omega = I\omega$. So the $L = I\omega$ from Physics 1 is this same definition, summed.
This is why a ball thrown at a door far from its hinges swings it more than one thrown near the hinge, and why Collisions with Rotation conserve angular momentum about a pivot.

blocks.html: Conservation of Angular Momentum kept $L$ constant for a spinning skater. Here a particle with Angular Momentum of a Particle hits an object that can only turn about a pivot, whose moment of inertia comes from The Parallel-Axis Theorem.

During the brief impact, the pivot pushes on the rod; otherwise the rod's top would swing sideways along with its bottom. That push is an outside force, so linear momentum is not conserved. But the pivot's force acts at the pivot, where its lever arm is zero, so it exerts no torque about the pivot. Gravity's torque matters only over time, and the impact is very short. So angular momentum about the pivot is the conserved quantity.

For a ball (mass $m$, speed $v$) hitting a pivoted object at perpendicular distance $d$ from the pivot and sticking: $$mvd = (I_{\text{object}} + md^2)\,\omega.$$ Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision. After the impact, use energy conservation for any swing.

blocks.html: Rotational Kinetic Energy and Work by Torque said a torque turning something through $\Delta\theta$ does work $\tau\Delta\theta$. Work by a Variable Force and Angular Velocity and Acceleration with Calculus extend that to torques that change, and to the rate of work.

$$W = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \tau\,d\theta, \qquad P = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = \tau\omega, \qquad W_{\text{net}} = \Delta\left(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\right),$$ with angles in radians and $\omega$ in rad/s.

A force $F$ applied tangentially at radius $r$ moves its point of application along an arc $ds = r\,d\theta$. The work is $F\,ds = (Fr)\,d\theta = \tau\,d\theta$. Divide by $dt$ for the power: $\tau\,d\theta/dt = \tau\omega$. The work-energy theorem becomes $\int\tau_{\text{net}}\,d\theta = \Delta K_{\text{rot}}$, the turning version of The Work-Energy Theorem from Newton's Second Law.

blocks.html: Multiplying the torque by an angle in degrees, or by an arc length. Turning $5\ \text{N·m}$ through $90^\circ$ does $5 \times \pi/2 = 7.85\ \text{J}$, not $450\ \text{J}$. And torque times arc length has units of N·m², not joules. Check: in $W = \tau\theta$, the radian is what makes N·m of torque become N·m of energy.

Friction torques work the same way with a minus sign. A grinding wheel ($I = 0.5\ \text{kg·m}^2$) spinning at $40\ \text{rad/s}$ stores $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.5)(40)^2 = 400\ \text{J}$; if a $2\ \text{N·m}$ friction torque stops it, it turns through $400/2 = 200\ \text{rad}$, about 32 revolutions, before stopping.

Gears and bicycle gears trade torque for speed at nearly constant power: $P = \tau\omega$, so a gear that turns the wheel half as fast can deliver about twice the torque. That is why a low gear helps on a hill.

blocks.html: Rest one end of a spinning gyroscope's axle on a stand and let go. Instead of tipping over, it swings slowly around in a horizontal circle. Angular Momentum of a Particle gave $d\vec{L}/dt = \vec{\tau}$; here that vector equation does something surprising.

The spin gives the wheel a large angular momentum $\vec{L}$ along its axle, which is horizontal. Gravity pulls down on the wheel's center, a distance $r$ from the support, so its torque about the support is $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times M\vec{g}$: horizontal and perpendicular to $\vec{L}$. In a short time $dt$, $\vec{L}$ changes by $d\vec{L} = \vec{\tau}\,dt$, sideways. A sideways nudge to a vector turns it without changing its length, through an angle $d\phi = \dfrac{dL}{L} = \dfrac{\tau\,dt}{L}$. So the axle sweeps around at $$\Omega = \dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = \dfrac{\tau}{L} = \dfrac{Mgr}{I\omega_s}.$$

A fast-spinning gyroscope supported at one end precesses at $\Omega = \dfrac{\tau}{L} = \dfrac{Mgr}{I\omega_s}$: the faster the spin, the slower the precession. The torque changes the direction of $\vec{L}$, not its size. (This holds when the spin is fast, $\Omega \ll \omega_s$.)

blocks.html: Expecting the spinning top or gyroscope to fall over like a non-spinning one. Without spin, $L$ starts at zero, and the torque builds angular momentum in its own direction: the wheel tips down. With a large spin $\vec{L}$, the same torque adds only a small sideways change to a big vector, which turns it. Check the directions: $d\vec{L}$ points along $\vec{\tau}$, and $\vec{\tau}$ is horizontal, so the axle moves sideways, not down. As friction slows the spin, $\Omega$ grows and the motion eventually becomes a fall.

Earth itself precesses: the Sun's and Moon's pulls on its equatorial bulge make its spin axis trace a circle about once every 26,000 years, slowly changing which star sits near the north celestial pole.

blocks.html: Rotational Equilibrium set the two conditions for an object at rest: zero net force and zero net torque about any point. With Static Friction and the vector torques of Torque as a Cross Product, you can solve ladders, hinged beams and hanging signs. The Book Cart lab lets you feel what happens when the balance fails.

For a rigid body in equilibrium: $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$ and $\sum\tau = 0$ about any point. Choose the pivot where the most unknown forces act: their torques vanish, often leaving one equation with one unknown.

If the net force is zero, the net torque is the same about every point: moving the pivot by $\vec{a}$ changes each $\vec{r}$ to $\vec{r} - \vec{a}$, and the total torque changes by $-\vec{a}\times\sum\vec{F} = 0$. So you are free to pick the most convenient point. A force through the pivot has zero lever arm, so it drops out of the torque equation, which is how a smart choice removes unknowns you don't need.

blocks.html: Gravitational Field Strength used $g = GM/r^2$ for a planet, as if all its mass sat at one point. Newton proved that this is exactly right outside a sphere, and found what happens inside. The proof is a single integral, made easy by Substitution in Definite Integrals.

Take a thin uniform shell of mass $M$ and radius $R$, and a point P a distance $r$ from its center. Slice the shell into rings around the line to P. The ring at angle $\theta$ has mass $dM = \tfrac{M}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta$, all of it a distance $s$ from P, where $s^2 = r^2 + R^2 - 2rR\cos\theta$. By symmetry only the pull along the line to the center survives, so $$g = \int \dfrac{G\,dM}{s^2}\cdot\dfrac{r - R\cos\theta}{s}.$$ Now substitute $s$ for $\theta$: $2s\,ds = 2rR\sin\theta\,d\theta$, and $r - R\cos\theta = \dfrac{s^2 + r^2 - R^2}{2r}$. The integral becomes $$g = \dfrac{GM}{4r^2R}\int\left(1 + \dfrac{r^2 - R^2}{s^2}\right)ds.$$ Outside the shell, $s$ runs from $r - R$ to $r + R$ and the integral is $4R$, so $g = GM/r^2$. Inside, $s$ runs from $R - r$ to $R + r$ and the integral is exactly $0$.

Shell theorem. A uniform spherical shell pulls on an outside mass as if all its mass were at its center, and exerts no net pull at all on a mass inside it. So for a uniform solid sphere: $$g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2} \;(r \ge R), \qquad g = \dfrac{GM}{R^3}r = g_s\dfrac{r}{R} \;(r \le R).$$ Inside, only the mass closer to the center counts; $g$ grows from zero at the center to its largest value at the surface.

blocks.q: Drop a ball into a frictionless, airless tunnel straight through a uniform Earth. How long until it reaches the other side?

So the motion is simple harmonic with $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g_s}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{6.37 \times 10^{6}}{9.8}} = 5070\ \text{s} \approx 84\ \text{min}$$
The other side is half a period away: about 42 minutes.

blocks.html: Thinking gravity is strongest at Earth's center, where you're "closest to all the mass." At the center, the mass pulls equally in every direction, and the pulls cancel: $g = 0$. Check with the shell theorem: on the way down, every shell above you stops pulling at all, so less and less mass is left below you.

The real Earth is not uniform: its iron core is much denser than its rocky mantle. Because of that, $g$ actually changes little on the way down through the mantle and is largest near the top of the core, before falling to zero at the center. The shell theorem still holds for each spherical layer.

blocks.html: Satellites in Orbit found the speed of a circular orbit, and Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Speed gave the potential energy $U = -GMm/r$. Put them together and orbital energy has a surprise in it. Explore it in the Orbit Lab.

In a circular orbit gravity supplies the centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$, so $mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{r}$ and $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} = -\tfrac{1}{2}U.$$ Adding, $E = K + U = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$. A larger orbit has a less negative $E$ (more energy) but a smaller $K$ (less speed): its $U$ rises by twice as much as its $K$ falls.

For a circular orbit of radius $r$: $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}, \qquad K = -E, \qquad U = 2E.$$ Moving to a higher orbit takes energy, $\Delta E = \dfrac{GMm}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)$, yet the satellite ends up slower, $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$.

The energy went into climbing out of the gravity well, which raises $U$ a lot; part of it even came out of the kinetic energy. Check with $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$: the Moon, far out, moves about 1 km/s; the space station, close in, about 7.7 km/s.

A strange consequence: air drag on a low satellite takes energy away, so $E$ becomes more negative and the orbit shrinks, and on the smaller orbit the satellite moves faster. Drag speeds it up, because gravity does more positive work during the slow spiral inward than drag does negative work.
The total energy is negative for every bound orbit and zero exactly at escape. For an ellipse, $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a}$ with $a$ the semi-major axis; you'll derive that in Speed on an Elliptical Orbit.

blocks.html: Kepler found from Tycho Brahe's measurements that a planet's line to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Angular Momentum of a Particle shows why, using only one fact about gravity: it points straight at the Sun. See it in the Orbit Lab. It builds on Satellites in Orbit.

Gravity on a planet points along $-\vec{r}$, from the planet to the Sun. Its torque about the Sun is $\vec{r}\times\vec{F} = 0$, because the two vectors are parallel. So $\vec{L} = m\,\vec{r}\times\vec{v}$ is constant. In a short time $dt$ the line from the Sun sweeps a thin triangle with sides $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{v}\,dt$, of area $$dA = \tfrac{1}{2}|\vec{r}\times\vec{v}\,dt| = \dfrac{L}{2m}\,dt.$$ So $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{L}{2m}$ is constant: equal areas in equal times.

Any central force conserves angular momentum, which is Kepler's second law: $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{L}{2m}$ is constant. At the nearest and farthest points the velocity is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$, so $$r_pv_p = r_av_a:$$ a planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion.

On an ellipse the distance changes, and to keep $rv\sin\phi$ constant the speed must rise as the distance falls. Check at the two ends: $v_pr_p = v_ar_a$ with $r_p < r_a$ forces $v_p > v_a$.

Nothing here used the inverse-square law: equal areas hold for any force that points toward a fixed center. The inverse square is what makes the orbit an ellipse and fixes the period, as in Kepler's Third Law from Newton.

blocks.html: Kepler's third law says the square of a planet's period is proportional to the cube of its orbit's size. Satellites in Orbit has everything needed to derive it, and the derivation turns it into a scale for weighing planets and stars.

For a circular orbit of radius $r$ and period $T$, the speed is $v = 2\pi r/T$, and gravity supplies the centripetal force: $$\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{4\pi^2mr}{T^2}.$$ The satellite's mass $m$ cancels, leaving $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$. Newton also showed that the same formula holds for an ellipse with $r$ replaced by the semi-major axis $a$.

$$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3.$$ It doesn't depend on the orbiting body's mass (when that is small compared with $M$), and $r$ is measured from the center of the central body. Solved for $M$: $M = \dfrac{4\pi^2r^3}{GT^2}$, which weighs a planet from any moon's orbit.

blocks.html: If the orbiting body is not small, both bodies circle their common center of mass, and the law becomes $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2a^3}{G(M + m)}$. For the Moon around Earth that matters at about the 1% level; for Io around Jupiter it is negligible. The same law with $a$ in AU, $T$ in years and masses in solar masses reads $T^2 = a^3/(M + m)$, which is how astronomers weigh stars in binary systems.

Using the altitude instead of the distance from the center, or putting the satellite's mass into the formula. A satellite 400 km up is $6.77 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$ from the center, not $4 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m}$; using the altitude gives a period of a few minutes, far too short. And the satellite's mass canceled in the derivation. Check: a geostationary orbit needs $T = 1$ sidereal day, which gives $r = 42\,164\ \text{km}$ from the center, about 35,800 km up.

blocks.html: On an elliptical orbit (Ellipses), the speed changes all the way around. Orbital Energy and Kepler's Second Law from Angular Momentum give one formula for the speed anywhere, and it is the tool for planning trips between planets. Try transfers in the Orbit Lab.

At the nearest point $r_p$ and farthest point $r_a$ the velocity is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$, so angular momentum gives $r_pv_p = r_av_a$. Energy gives $\tfrac{1}{2}v_p^2 - \dfrac{GM}{r_p} = \tfrac{1}{2}v_a^2 - \dfrac{GM}{r_a}$ (per kilogram). Substituting $v_a = v_pr_p/r_a$ and solving, the total energy per kilogram comes out as $-\dfrac{GM}{r_p + r_a} = -\dfrac{GM}{2a}$, where $a = \tfrac{1}{2}(r_p + r_a)$ is the semi-major axis. Energy is the same everywhere on the orbit, so at any distance $r$: $\tfrac{1}{2}v^2 - \dfrac{GM}{r} = -\dfrac{GM}{2a}$.

The vis-viva equation: $$v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac{2}{r} - \dfrac{1}{a}\right).$$ For a circle ($r = a$) it gives $v^2 = GM/r$. A Hohmann transfer between circular orbits $r_1$ and $r_2$ uses an ellipse with $a = \tfrac{1}{2}(r_1 + r_2)$: one burn at $r_1$ to get onto it, a second at $r_2$ to circularize.

blocks.html: Graphs of Simple Harmonic Motion showed that a mass on a spring traces sine and cosine curves. With Derivatives of Trig Functions and Higher Derivatives we can see why: Newton's second law for a spring is a differential equation, and cosine is the function that solves it.

For a mass $m$ on a spring of stiffness $k$, with $x$ measured from equilibrium, $F = -kx$, so $$m\ddot{x} = -kx \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ddot{x} = -\dfrac{k}{m}x.$$ We need a function whose second derivative is a negative multiple of itself. Try $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$: then $\dot{x} = -A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi)$ and $\ddot{x} = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t + \phi) = -\omega^2x$. It works exactly when $\omega^2 = k/m$, for any amplitude $A$ and phase $\phi$.

Simple harmonic motion obeys $\ddot{x} = -\omega^2x$, solved by $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ with $$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}, \qquad f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}, \qquad T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$ The greatest speed is $A\omega$ (at equilibrium) and the greatest acceleration $A\omega^2$ (at the turning points). The period doesn't depend on the amplitude.

Energy gives a quick check. With $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$, $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$ at every instant (use $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ and $m\omega^2 = k$). So the speed at position $x$ is $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$: largest at $x = 0$, zero at $x = \pm A$.

The same equation, $\ddot{q} = -\omega^2q$, describes a pendulum's small swings, an LC circuit's charge and a vibrating molecule. Near any stable equilibrium, as in Potential Energy Diagrams, small motions are simple harmonic.

blocks.html: The Equation of Simple Harmonic Motion found that $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ solves the spring equation for any $A$ and $\phi$. The physics picks them: where the mass starts and how fast it is moving. Finding $\phi$ needs Inverse Trig Functions, with care about quadrants.

At $t = 0$: $x_0 = A\cos\phi$ and $v_0 = \dot{x}(0) = -A\omega\sin\phi$. So $\cos\phi = \dfrac{x_0}{A}$ and $\sin\phi = -\dfrac{v_0}{A\omega}$. Squaring and adding (since $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$): $$A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + \left(\dfrac{v_0}{\omega}\right)^2}.$$ The ratio gives $\tan\phi = -\dfrac{v_0}{\omega x_0}$, but a tangent alone can't tell quadrant I from III or II from IV. The signs of $\cos\phi$ (same as $x_0$) and $\sin\phi$ (opposite to $v_0$) decide.

$$A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + (v_0/\omega)^2}, \qquad \cos\phi = \dfrac{x_0}{A}, \quad \sin\phi = -\dfrac{v_0}{A\omega}.$$ Equivalently, $x(t) = x_0\cos\omega t + \dfrac{v_0}{\omega}\sin\omega t$, which needs no phase at all.

blocks.html: Hang a mass from a spring and it stretches, then bounces about its new resting point. Does gravity change the motion that The Equation of Simple Harmonic Motion described? Only where it is centered.

Take $y$ downward from the spring's natural length. Newton's second law: $m\ddot{y} = mg - ky$. At equilibrium $\ddot{y} = 0$, so the stretch there is $d = mg/k$. Now measure from that point: $y = d + u$. Then $$m\ddot{u} = mg - k(d + u) = (mg - kd) - ku = -ku.$$ The constant force of gravity is exactly cancelled by the extra stretch $kd$, leaving the same equation as a horizontal spring.

A vertical spring oscillates about its stretched equilibrium $d = mg/k$ with the same period as without gravity: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{d}{g}}.$$ Gravity shifts the center of the motion; it doesn't change how stiff the motion is.
