blocks.title: Stretch and period
blocks.q: A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ mass hangs from a spring with $k = 20\ \text{N/m}$. Find the equilibrium stretch and the period.
steps: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.5/20} = 0.993\ \text{s}$, the same as on a horizontal track.
Also $2\pi\sqrt{d/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.245/9.8} = 0.993\ \text{s}$: the stretch alone tells you the period.

blocks.title: Let go at the natural length
blocks.q: The same mass is hooked onto the unstretched spring and released from rest. How far does it fall, and what is the largest spring force?
steps: It starts at rest $d = 0.245\ \text{m}$ above equilibrium, so its amplitude is $A = d$.
It turns around $d$ below equilibrium: a total drop of $2d = 0.49\ \text{m}$.
There the stretch is $2d$, so the spring pulls with $k(2d) = 2mg = 9.8\ \text{N}$, twice the weight.
blocks.a: It drops $0.49\ \text{m}$; the spring force peaks at $9.8\ \text{N}$.

blocks.html: Energy tells the same story. Measured from the stretched equilibrium, the spring energy and the gravitational energy together add up to $\tfrac{1}{2}ku^2$ plus a constant (the linear terms in $u$ cancel because $kd = mg$). So the energy sloshes between $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}ku^2$, exactly as on a horizontal spring.

Thinking gravity makes a hanging spring oscillate faster or slower. Gravity is the same at every point of the motion, so it can't supply a restoring force; only the spring's extra stretch or squeeze does. Check: the period formula $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ has no $g$ in it. (A pendulum is different: there gravity is the restoring force, so $g$ appears.)

blocks.html: Period of a Pendulum gave $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ for a small bob on a string. A swinging bar, a leg or a door knocker is a rigid body: its mass is spread out, so we need The Parallel-Axis Theorem, the torque form of Newton's law, and the small-angle trick from Linear Approximation and Differentials. It builds on The Equation of Simple Harmonic Motion. See pendulums keep time in the Pendulums and Resonance lab.

A rigid body hangs from a pivot with its center of mass a distance $d$ below. Tilted by $\theta$, gravity acting at the center of mass gives a torque $\tau = -mgd\sin\theta$ about the pivot. Newton's law for rotation: $$I\ddot{\theta} = -mgd\sin\theta.$$ For small angles (in radians), $\sin\theta \approx \theta$, the linear approximation near 0, so $\ddot{\theta} = -\dfrac{mgd}{I}\theta$: simple harmonic motion with $\omega^2 = \dfrac{mgd}{I}$.

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}},$$ with $I$ about the pivot and $d$ from the pivot to the center of mass. A simple pendulum is the special case $I = mL^2$, $d = L$. The formula holds for small swings; larger swings take slightly longer.

blocks.title: A swinging rod
blocks.q: A uniform meter stick swings from one end. Find its period for small swings.
steps: A simple pendulum of length $\tfrac{2}{3}L$ has the same period: some of the rod's mass is close to the pivot and swings in a smaller arc.

blocks.title: A disk on a nail
blocks.q: A uniform disk of radius $0.20\ \text{m}$ hangs on a nail through a point on its rim. Find its period.

blocks.html: Using the whole length of a swinging rod as the pendulum length, as in $2\pi\sqrt{L/g} = 2.01\ \text{s}$ for the meter stick. A rod isn't a bob on a string: its mass is spread from the pivot to the tip. Check: put $I$ about the pivot and $d$ from the pivot to the center of mass into $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgd)}$; for a rod pivoted at its end, $d = L/2$.

The small-angle period is very close for modest swings: at a $30^\circ$ amplitude the true period is only about 1.7% longer, and at $10^\circ$ about 0.2%. That near-independence from amplitude is why pendulums made good clocks.

blocks.html: Real oscillations die out. Add a drag force like the one in Linear Drag and Terminal Velocity to the spring of The Equation of Simple Harmonic Motion, and the cosine gets wrapped in a shrinking exponential, the shape you graphed in Damped Oscillation.

With drag $-b\dot{x}$: $m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = 0$. Try $x = e^{rt}$: $mr^2 + br + k = 0$, so $$r = -\dfrac{b}{2m} \pm \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{b}{2m}\right)^2 - \dfrac{k}{m}}.$$ If $b^2 < 4mk$ the square root is imaginary, $\pm i\omega_d$, and the real solutions are $e^{-bt/2m}\cos(\omega_dt + \phi)$: oscillation inside a decaying envelope. If $b^2 = 4mk$ there is one repeated root (critical damping); if $b^2 > 4mk$, two negative real roots (overdamped): no oscillation at all.

Underdamped ($b < 2\sqrt{km}$): $$x = A_0e^{-bt/2m}\cos(\omega_dt + \phi), \qquad \omega_d = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m} - \left(\dfrac{b}{2m}\right)^2}.$$ The amplitude falls by half every $\dfrac{2m\ln 2}{b}$, and the energy as $e^{-bt/m}$. Critical damping, $b_c = 2\sqrt{km}$, returns to equilibrium fastest without overshooting; more damping (overdamped) returns more slowly.

blocks.q: A $1\ \text{kg}$ mass on a spring ($k = 100\ \text{N/m}$) has $b = 2\ \text{N·s/m}$. How long until the amplitude halves, and what is $\omega_d$?

blocks.title: Designing a door closer
blocks.q: What damping makes the same system critically damped?
steps: With this damping, a pushed door swings shut quickly without banging past the frame.

blocks.html: Thinking a critically damped system swings once before it stops. Released from rest, it never crosses equilibrium: critical damping is the boundary between oscillating and not. Any overshoot means the system is (slightly) underdamped. Check the roots of $mr^2 + br + k = 0$: when they are real, there is no cosine in the solution, so nothing to swing.

blocks.html: Push a swing at the right moment of each cycle and small pushes build a big swing. Damped Oscillations gives the losses that stop this growth. You can push a swing in rhythm in the Pendulums and Resonance lab.

Add a driving force: $m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = F_0\cos\omega t$. After the starting transient dies away (it decays like the damped motion), the system settles into motion at the driving frequency: $x = A\cos(\omega t - \delta)$. Substituting and matching the cosine and sine terms gives $$A(\omega) = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + (b\omega/m)^2}}, \qquad \omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}.$$ When $\omega$ is near $\omega_0$, the first term in the root nearly vanishes, and only damping keeps the amplitude finite.

Driven near its natural frequency, a lightly damped oscillator responds strongly: at $\omega = \omega_0$, $A = \dfrac{F_0}{b\omega_0}$. Far below, $A \approx F_0/k$ (just the static stretch); far above, the response is small. The ratio of the resonant amplitude to the static one is $Q = \dfrac{m\omega_0}{b}$: less damping, sharper and taller peak.

opts.task: Move the driving frequency through $\omega_0 = 4\ \text{rad/s}$ and watch the steady amplitude on the resonance curve.

blocks.cap: A driven, damped spring: the steady amplitude against the driving frequency peaks near $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m} = 4\ \text{rad/s}$.

blocks.title: At resonance
blocks.q: A $1\ \text{kg}$ mass on a spring ($k = 100\ \text{N/m}$, $b = 1\ \text{N·s/m}$) is driven by $F_0\cos\omega t$ with $F_0 = 2\ \text{N}$ at $\omega = \omega_0$. Find the steady amplitude and compare it with the static stretch.
steps: Static stretch: $F_0/k = 0.02\ \text{m}$. Resonance multiplies it by $Q = m\omega_0/b = 10$.

blocks.title: Off resonance
blocks.q: Same system, driven at $\omega = 8\ \text{rad/s}$. Find the amplitude.
steps: $A = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{36^2 + 8^2}} = \dfrac{2}{36.9} = 0.054\ \text{m}$, about a quarter of the resonant value.

blocks.html: Thinking any repeated push in rhythm makes the amplitude grow without limit. Each push adds energy, but a bigger swing also loses more energy per cycle to friction and air; the amplitude levels off where the two balance. Check the formula: at $\omega = \omega_0$ the amplitude is $F_0/(b\omega_0)$, finite for any real damping $b > 0$.

The timing matters as much as the size. Driven slowly, the mass moves in step with the force; driven fast, it moves opposite to it; at resonance the displacement lags the force by a quarter cycle, so the force is in step with the velocity. That is exactly when the force does the most positive work each cycle, as when you push a swing while it moves away from you.

Resonance is useful (tuning a radio, a child on a swing) and sometimes a hazard, which is why engineers add damping to buildings and bridges and avoid natural frequencies near common driving frequencies, such as footsteps or machinery.
